blocks.text: Logistic regression is a powerful tool used when we want to predict an outcome that can be categorized as “yes” or “no”.

Example: Let's say we want to determine whether a student will pass or fail an exam based on the number of hours they study. Instead of giving a specific score, logistic regression helps us find the probability of passing.
Understanding Logistic Regression

Logistic regression is different from linear regression because it doesn't predict exact numbers. Instead, it provides a probability value between 0 and 1. This means it tells us how likely something is to happen.
Example: If the model predicts a probability of 0.85 for passing the exam, it means there's an 85% chance the student will pass based on their study hours.

Creating the Logistic Function
The logistic regression model gives us an equation like this:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed equation leaves out e and the minus sign in the denominator. The logistic function is P(pass) = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + β₁ × Hours Studied)), as the next equations use it.
In this equation:

items: P(Pass) is the probability of passing the exam.
e is the base of the natural logarithm.
β₀ is the intercept of the model, which represents the log-odds of passing when no hours are studied.
β₁ is the coefficient for the number of hours studied, showing how much the log-odds of passing changes with each additional hour.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: With β₀ = 1 and β₁ = 0.6, 1 + 0.6 × 5 = 4 and P = 1 / (1 + e⁻⁴) ≈ 0.98, a 98% chance. The book's 0.83 is the value for 1 hour of study (1 + 0.6 × 1 = 1.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: For 4 hours, 1 + 0.6 × 4 = 3.4 and P = 1 / (1 + e^−3.4) ≈ 0.97, a 97% chance. The book's 0.73 is the value for 0 hours (1 / (1 + e⁻¹)).
